text: Is dependency confusion attack possible with hardcoded path On a private bug bounty, i encountered the below scenario and I was wondering whether it was possible to perform a dependency confusion attack, or not. The package.json looks like this: { "name": "project_name", "private": true, "dependencies": { "some-package": "^X.XX.XX", "some-other-package": "^X.XX.XX", "another-one": "^X.XX.XX", }, "version": "X.XX.XX", "devDependencies": { "some-package": "^X.XX.XX", "some-other-package": "^X.XX.XX", "vulnerable-package": "file:path/to/index.js" The (devDepedency) vulnerable-package is not tied to a scope (i.e., not belonging to any npm organization) and as you can see it refers directly to a directory within the repo of the project. Obviously, an attacker can claim the name of the package and upload malicious code on npm, but I tested using different package managers, it seems the only case where the dependency confusion attack can happen is by: Running explicitly {npm|pnpm|yarn} {add|install} vulnerable-package Not having the package.json in the current working directory Which, i think you will agree, significantly lower the criticality and the likelihood of the attack. The attack originally relies on the package manager fetching an higher version and/or the public registry taking precedence on a private one. Here, the victim needs to explicitly mention the vulnerable package, without having the package.json in the current working directory. Is there any case i didn’t think of?
label: risk_assessment
note: Propuesta para revisar: Evalúa posibilidad de ataque por dependencia

text: Is this CSP issue a false positive? I just ran into a weird situation with Burp Suite Professional. They unfortunately discontinued their forum, so I'm asking here. It starts with the following Content-Security Policy (CSP): Content-Security-Policy: default-src * http://*:* https://*:* data: 'self' ; img-src http://*:* https://*:* blob: data: 'self' ; script-src 'self' ; object-src 'self'; style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' ; Burp Suite Complains about this as follows: The policy allows global wildcard URLs which allows arbitrary scripts to be executed. The policy allows data: URLs which allows arbitrary scripts to be executed. As you can see the values Burp is flagging are in the default-src directive. This however seems wrong to me, since default-src is only a fallback for missing directives so in this case script-src self would block XSS attempts and default-src would be ignored. or to quote Mozilla Developer Network: "The HTTP Content-Security-Policy (CSP) default-src directive serves as a fallback for the other CSP fetch directives. For each of the following directives that are absent, the user agent looks for the default-src directive and uses this value for it. ... If there are other directives specified, default-src does not influence them." Did I miss anything or is this finding simply a false-positive due to simplistic matching logic?
label: risk_assessment
note: Propuesta para revisar: Evalúa si un hallazgo CSP es vulnerabilidad real

text: De-anonymization of VPN use through broken killswitch? This answer to a question about how to make a killswitch for use with a VPN states "don't simply whitelist port 1194 or you will allow trivial deanonymization" and this answer to a similar question states that adding the following rules to iptables "will allow deanonymization because it allows any connection over port 1194, not just traffic originating from OpenVPN" (for the sake of brevity, assume default table policy is to DROP packets) iptables -A OUTPUT -p udp --dport 1194 -j ACCEPT iptables -A INPUT -p udp --sport 1194 -j ACCEPT Although the first line could be narrowed by adding the destination VPN's IP address, even without, surely it is not a vulnerability(?). I think the second of these two lines would be better replaced by a canonical ACCEPT rule for conntrack states ESTABLISHED and RELATED , otherwise an attacker can freely connect from their port 1194 and probe the device, though absent some known vulnerability, I don't know specifically what that achieves. My question is if it's true that this allows deanonymization, what exactly that means (and to what extent) and how an attacker would achieve that goal. Please do not discuss traffic correlation, TCP fingerprinting or other VPN weaknesses outside the scope of firewall issues. Or if the firewall rules are TCP instead of UDP, would that give an attacker something concrete for this supposed de-anonymization to work?
label: risk_assessment
note: Propuesta para revisar: Evalúa riesgo de desanonimización por reglas VPN

text: Using my own CA for home VPN -- too much or not enough? I recently set up a "homelab," so to speak, with several machines that have personal data and applications that I'd like to be able to use on the go. I set up a KeepassXC database secured by a Yubikey and I sync the database file via a home installation of Nextcloud to my phone for password management. What I'd like to do is set up a VPN, but I find myself wondering whether using the LetsEncrypt functionality and OpenVPN server on my ASUS-Merlin router is "safe enough." I thought that maybe, since I manage all devices on this network, I'd use my own private CA and then install it on all of the devices (perhaps via KeepassXC), so that unless someone has a device with that cert, OpenVPN won't let them into my network. That of course made me wonder, hey, couldn't I do that for my wifi access too, and down the rabbit hole I went. Of course, this is all based off of experience from work, where people are pretty paranoid, and rightfully so, about VPN management. But for a home user like me, is "the juice not worth the squeeze?" Am I really screwing this up? Or if not, how much more protection can I gain if I use a private PKI/CA infrastructure like that? It's a fun project, but if I get 2% better protection from it, then it's not worth it. A similar question was posted here , though I'm looking more for a quick "risk analysis" ranging from "You're a moron" to "Hey, if it's fun, maybe 15% less chance of someone getting in, so why not?"
label: risk_assessment
note: Requests a risk analysis of using a private CA for a home VPN.
